description.summary: A female tree spirit of Thai (and Lao and Cambodian) folklore, believed to inhabit clumps of the wild banana Musa acuminata (kluai tani). She is one of the best-known Nang Mai (tree spirits) and is generally benevolent, though said to harm men who have wronged women.
description.full: Nang Tani (Thai: นางตานี, 'Lady of Tani') is a female tree spirit of Thai, Lao, and Cambodian folklore, also known as Phi Tani ('Ghost of Tani') or Phrai Tani ('Nymph of Tani'). She is one of the most prominent Nang Mai (Thai female tree spirits) and is bound to clumps of the wild banana Musa acuminata, called kluai tani in Thai — a non-cultivated species whose fruit is inedible, growing at village outskirts and field edges and traditionally avoided near homes for that reason. The spirit is described as a beautiful young woman with a greenish complexion that blends with foliage, red lips compared to ripe ivy gourd fruit, abundant black unbound hair, and a green traditional Thai costume; her feet hover slightly above the ground, and modern depictions sometimes show her lower body fading into wisps from the trunk of the banana. Nang Tani is generally benevolent — said to remain hidden within her tree, become visible on full-moon nights, and even offer alms to passing Buddhist monks — but folklore warns she may harm men who have wronged women. Cutting a tree from her clump is believed to bring misfortune. Devotional practice includes tying coloured satin cloth around the tree, leaving sweets, incense, and flowers, and wearing protective amulets bearing her image. The figure has a strong presence in 20th- and 21st-century Thai cinema, beginning with the 1967 classic Nang Phrai Tani.

etymology.origin: Thai นาง (nang, 'lady') + ตานี (tani), the name of the wild banana species (Musa acuminata, kluai tani) she inhabits.
etymology.first_use: Long-standing Thai folk tradition; well-attested in 20th-century Thai popular culture.

range.description: Folklore of Nang Tani is concentrated in Thailand and extends to neighboring Laos and Cambodia.

origins.cultural_roots: Thai animist tradition of Nang Mai (female tree spirits) integrated with Theravada Buddhist practice.
origins.earliest_accounts: Documented in modern Thai folkloric writing and 20th-century popular culture; long-standing oral tradition.
origins.folklore_connections: Belongs to the broader Nang Mai class of Thai tree spirits and is comparable to other Southeast Asian banana-tree spirits, including the Ryukyuan bashōnosei.

history.modern_era: Nang Tani is a fixture of contemporary Thai popular culture, appearing in horror films, comics, storybooks, and even Thai television advertising.

paranormal.name: Animist tree spirit
paranormal.description: Traditional Thai animist understanding of Nang Tani as a real spirit inhabiting wild banana clumps, generally benevolent but capable of punishing wrongdoers.

skeptical.name: Cultural-ecological / domestic taboo function
skeptical.description: Anthropological reading: avoidance of planting kluai tani near homes, and the prohibition on cutting it, function as cultural taboos that constrain behavior in marginal village spaces.
proponents: Folklorists and anthropologists of Thai religion

folklore.beliefs: Wild banana (kluai tani) is treated with caution: its inedible fruit and ghost-association lead Thai households to avoid planting it near homes.
